cards.title: Trump’s Iran Trap: Escalation Risks Domestic Blowback, Concession Risks Strategic Weakness
cards.background: A fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran, in place since April 8, is under strain as peace proposals stall and both sides harden their positions. Trump has said the ceasefire is on "life support," while US officials have hinted at renewed military action; Iran has rejected US demands to dismantle its nuclear programme and wants sanctions relief plus recognition of its influence over the Strait of Hormuz. The article says the conflict has already involved five weeks of US bombing, Iranian missile and drone attacks on the UAE, and disruption fears around a chokepoint that carries roughly one-fifth of global energy exports.

prop_args.thesis: Trump is structurally better off cutting a deal with Iran than pursuing renewed escalation, because the domestic, military, and regional costs of war are rising faster than the strategic gains.
mechanisms: First, escalation creates immediate domestic political punishment. This is because (1) two-thirds of Americans in the Reuters/Ipsos survey said Trump has not given a clear rationale for the war, (2) the same share say they are already feeling financial strain as gas, oil, and fertiliser prices rise, and (3) Trump’s approval is only 36 percent heading into midterm elections, so a prolonged war becomes a direct liability for congressional control.

Second, renewed strikes are unlikely to coerce Tehran into surrendering its core positions. Three reasons: one, Iran has already shown higher resilience and a greater tolerance for pain than Washington expected; two, its enrichment infrastructure, proxy networks, and ballistic missile arsenal remain intact enough to preserve bargaining power; three, Tehran’s leadership now believes the war failed to force strategic concessions, so more bombing may harden rather than soften its stance.

Third, a negotiated de-escalation is strategically preferable because it preserves US force readiness and stabilises energy markets. This matters because (1) five weeks of bombing have already reduced US ammunition stockpiles and readiness for other contingencies, especially China, (2) the Strait of Hormuz carries roughly a fifth of global energy exports, so even limited disruption amplifies inflation globally, and (3) Trump can frame a partial deal as a victory while quietly prioritising the nuclear file over the harder issue of Hormuz.

opp_args.thesis: Trump should maintain pressure and be willing to escalate, because conceding to Iran would reward coercion, weaken deterrence, and leave Tehran stronger in the long run.
mechanisms: First, backing down signals that armed resistance works. One, Iran has already used missiles and drones to target the UAE after US moves on Hormuz, showing it can impose costs; two, if Washington responds by accepting Iranian demands, it validates proxy warfare and brinkmanship; three, that precedent encourages Iran and other regional actors to escalate first and negotiate later.

Second, a tougher line may be the only way to stop Iran from preserving a latent nuclear breakout capability. One, Iran’s enriched uranium remains in-country and its enrichment sites have not been dismantled; two, Tehran explicitly rejects dismantling its nuclear programme; three, if the US prioritises diplomacy without leverage, Iran can buy time, retain capabilities, and emerge with a stronger deterrent posture.

Third, escalation can restore US credibility with allies and adversaries. One, Israel and Gulf partners need assurance that the US will not abandon them under pressure; two, if Trump accepts Iranian influence over Hormuz or lifts sanctions too easily, it signals weakness across the region; three, a credible threat of force may extract a better deal than negotiations alone.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether coercion actually changes Iranian behaviour or just imposes costs on the US and its allies. Prop has the structural advantage because the article shows Iran has already absorbed pressure, while the US faces clearer domestic, economic, and readiness constraints; Opp only wins if it proves escalation can still produce a materially better end state than a messy compromise.

THP a world in which major powers negotiate with adversaries after limited conflict rather than pursue escalation

cards.title: Civilian Mass Casualties in Nigeria and Chad Expose the Costs of Counterinsurgency Airpower
cards.background: On 13 May 2026, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk called for independent investigations into separate air attacks by Nigerian and Chadian forces that reportedly killed more than 100 civilians. Amnesty International said a Nigerian airstrike on 10 May hit a crowded market in Tumfa village, Zamfara state, killing at least 100 civilians, while reports also alleged Chadian jets struck Boko Haram camps on remote islands in the Lake Chad marshlands, killing dozens including fishermen. Nigeria’s defence headquarters denied credible evidence of civilian casualties and said its strike targeted a 'confirmed high-level gathering' of terrorists.

prop_args.thesis: Independent investigations and accountability are necessary because unchecked air campaigns against insurgents systematically kill civilians and worsen the conflict.
mechanisms: First, accountability reduces repeat civilian harm. This is because (1) airstrikes are high-variance tools that rely on imperfect intelligence, (2) without external scrutiny militaries can classify every strike as a 'terrorist' success, and (3) the absence of consequences lowers the incentive to improve target verification, warning protocols, and post-strike review.

Second, civilian deaths fuel insurgent recruitment and local support for armed groups. Three reasons: one, when markets, fishermen, and villages are hit, communities see the state as an indiscriminate predator rather than a protector; two, insurgents can use the deaths as propaganda to frame themselves as defenders against state violence; three, fear and grievance push civilians toward cooperation, taxation compliance, or passive tolerance of Boko Haram/ISWAP and bandits.

Third, independent probes preserve state legitimacy and international humanitarian law norms. This matters because (1) Nigeria and Chad both rely on external military assistance and diplomatic support, (2) repeated allegations of massacre without investigation erode trust in the armed forces and the government, and (3) normalizing impunity in counterterrorism operations creates a precedent that civilian protection is optional whenever states invoke security threats.

opp_args.thesis: The priority should be operational freedom against insurgents, because over-legalizing counterterrorism can weaken states facing urgent and asymmetric threats.
mechanisms: First, insurgent groups exploit legal and political constraints to hide among civilians. One, Boko Haram and bandit groups operate in markets, islands, and remote villages where combatants and civilians are intermingled; two, demanding perfect certainty before striking can create safe havens for militants; three, delayed action allows armed groups to regroup, tax civilians, and expand territorial control.

Second, external investigations can undermine morale and command effectiveness. One, soldiers and commanders may become risk-averse if every strike triggers international scrutiny; two, this can reduce willingness to act in fast-moving battlefield conditions where split-second decisions matter; three, insurgents then gain a tactical advantage because the state is slower and less decisive than non-state actors.

Third, domestic institutions may be better placed than international actors to assess these incidents. One, local militaries have access to classified intelligence, battle damage assessments, and operational context that outsiders lack; two, foreign-led pressure can be perceived as politicized or neo-colonial, reducing cooperation from the state; three, if the goal is reform, internal military discipline and national courts may be more sustainable than UN-led condemnation.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between immediate civilian protection and the state’s ability to fight insurgents effectively. Prop wins if the round prioritizes long-run conflict reduction and rule-of-law legitimacy; opp wins if the round treats counterinsurgency urgency and intelligence uncertainty as overriding, because the costs of operational paralysis can be catastrophic in active war zones.

THBT states facing insurgencies should accept international oversight of military operations
THP a world where counterterrorism airstrikes require post-strike civilian harm review before public justification

cards.title: Democrats’ Defense of Racial Preferences Blocks Their Pivot to Class-Based Economic Populism
cards.background: The article argues that race-based affirmative action remains politically unpopular after the Supreme Court’s 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, which declared racial preferences in college admissions unlawful. It cites California’s 54–14 Assembly vote in February to put a constitutional change on the November ballot to allow racial preferences in K–12 education and higher-education scholarships, New York City’s new 375-page Racial Equity Plan, and Maryland Democrats overriding Gov. Wes Moore’s veto of reparations-study legislation. The piece also cites research by David Broockman and Joshua Kalla across 29 issue areas, claiming that moving to the center on racial preferences would be one of the most electorally beneficial shifts for Democrats.

prop_args.thesis: Democrats should abandon race-based preferences and replace them with class-based affirmative action because that is both electorally stronger and substantively fairer.
mechanisms: First, class-based targeting broadens the coalition Democrats can win. This is because (1) economically disadvantaged voters exist in every racial group, so the policy is legible as universal rather than factional; (2) swing voters are far more likely to support help based on need than race; and (3) the article cites Broockman and Kalla finding that moving to the center on racial preferences was the most electorally fruitful policy shift Democrats could make.

Second, race-based preferences create a symbolic backlash that hurts Democrats beyond the policy itself. Three reasons: one, many voters read racial preferences as preferential treatment rather than equal opportunity; two, Republicans can easily weaponize DEI and affirmative action as proof Democrats are out of touch; three, the issue is especially toxic in red-state and working-class districts where Democrats already hemorrhage support.

Third, class-based affirmative action is already proving more workable in practice. This matters because (1) after the 2023 Supreme Court ruling, top colleges increased Pell-eligible enrollment at 83 percent of schools with available data; (2) in the AP sample, MIT, Duke, and Smith all increased Pell representation by 25–35 percent; and (3) this shows institutions can preserve diversity and mobility goals without relying on legally vulnerable racial categories.

opp_args.thesis: Democrats should retain some race-conscious policies because class-only approaches miss the specific harms created by racial discrimination and would weaken efforts to remedy persistent inequality.
mechanisms: First, race and class are not interchangeable, so class-based targeting can under-capture disadvantage. One, Black and other minority students face discrimination, stereotyping, and network exclusion even when they are not the poorest; two, race-neutral poverty programs can leave out middle-income minority applicants who still face structural barriers; three, race-conscious policies are designed to address harms that are specifically racial, not merely economic.

Second, abandoning racial preferences may demobilize core Democratic constituencies and activists. One, many Black voters and civil-rights groups see race-conscious policy as a concrete commitment to racial justice; two, retreating on the issue can be framed as surrendering to conservative attacks on DEI; three, party elites may fear that once they concede on admissions and contracting, broader anti-racial-equity rollbacks become easier.

Third, the political downside may be overstated because voters care more about the economy than affirmative action. One, the article itself notes inflation, jobs, and health care usually outrank affirmative action in voter priorities; two, Democrats can absorb losses on a niche issue if they deliver on bread-and-butter economics; three, race-conscious policies may matter more as a moral signal to the base than as a decisive swing-voter issue.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether race-based preferences are a high-salience electoral liability or a necessary tool for racial justice. Prop has the structural advantage on broad coalition-building and legal durability, while Opp wins if they can prove class-only policy systematically misses racialized disadvantage and that base mobilization outweighs swing-voter costs.

cards.title: Targeted Billionaire Taxes Risk Normalizing Anti-Accumulation Politics Over Broad-Based Growth
cards.background: The article responds to left- and right-wing populist calls for targeted taxes on billionaires and the ultra-wealthy. It cites Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez saying, "You can’t earn a billion dollars," and notes that New York progressive Zohran Mamdani and a proposed California wealth tax reflect similar politics. The piece argues that this rhetoric misdiagnoses how wealth is created and sends the wrong message to aspiring workers and entrepreneurs.

prop_args.thesis: Targeted billionaire taxes are bad policy because they punish wealth creation at the top without fixing the real sources of inequality, which are low wages, weak mobility, and distorted opportunity.
mechanisms: First, they misidentify the problem. This is because (1) the binding constraint for most workers is not billionaire wealth itself but stagnant earnings and asset access, (2) taxing a tiny number of ultra-rich individuals does not materially raise broad middle-class incomes, and (3) it diverts political energy away from labor-market, education, and housing reforms that actually change distribution.

Second, they weaken incentives for entrepreneurship and capital formation. Three reasons: one, if the state signals that exceptional upside will be heavily clawed back, fewer founders and investors take high-risk bets; two, wealthy households are disproportionately the source of venture funding, philanthropy, and reinvested capital; three, uncertainty over confiscatory taxation encourages tax planning, relocation, and lower domestic investment.

Third, the rhetoric itself has negative dynamic effects on aspiration and social trust. This matters because it teaches young people that success is illegitimate rather than attainable, which (1) reduces effort and ambition, (2) increases zero-sum resentment between classes, and (3) makes future redistribution politics easier to justify even when they are economically inefficient.

opp_args.thesis: Targeted taxes on billionaires are justified because extreme wealth concentration distorts democracy and can be used to fund high-value public goods without materially harming the broader economy.
mechanisms: First, billionaires have outsized political power, so taxing them is a corrective rather than a punishment. One, concentrated wealth buys lobbying, media influence, and agenda-setting power; two, that influence can entrench monopoly rents and favorable tax treatment; three, reducing extreme wealth can therefore improve democratic responsiveness.

Second, the revenue can finance socially productive spending with high multiplier effects. One, wealth taxes can fund housing, childcare, health, or education; two, these programs raise labor-force participation and long-run productivity; three, the marginal utility of dollars is far higher when transferred from billionaires to liquidity-constrained households.

Third, the economic downside is often overstated because billionaire wealth is already partly illiquid and tax-avoidant. One, much of it is held in assets rather than consumption; two, sophisticated avoidance means current systems under-tax the ultra-rich anyway; three, well-designed taxes can capture rents without meaningfully reducing real investment.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether billionaire wealth is a symptom of healthy capitalism or a source of distortive power. Prop wins if the judge prioritizes growth, investment, and aspiration effects; Opp wins if they prove extreme concentration creates democratic and allocative harms that outweigh any marginal efficiency loss.

THBT governments should target billionaires with higher taxes

cards.title: German Shrinkflation Ruling Raises the Cost of Hidden Price Hikes for Consumer Brands
cards.background: A Bremen regional court ruled that Mondelēz misled consumers by reducing Milka Alpenmilch chocolate bars from 100g to 90g while keeping the same purple wrapper and product presentation. The case was brought by Hamburg consumer protection office VZHH, which argued the packaging created a misleading expectation; Mondelēz said it had disclosed the change on its website and social media and may appeal within one month. The bar’s price rose from €1.49 to €1.99 at the start of 2025, while chocolate prices in the UK rose 14.6% in the year to August 2025 amid cocoa supply shocks from poor West African harvests.

prop_args.thesis: Strict anti-shrinkflation enforcement improves market transparency and forces firms to compete on genuine prices rather than hidden deception.
mechanisms: First, it corrects information asymmetry between firms and consumers. This is because (1) most shoppers anchor on familiar packaging rather than checking grams every purchase, (2) firms exploit that inertia by keeping the same visual cues while quietly reducing quantity, and (3) mandatory, clear notices raise the salience of the real price per unit so consumers can make rational comparisons.

Second, it disciplines pricing behavior across the sector. Three reasons: one, if firms know they cannot hide quantity cuts, they are more likely to absorb cost shocks through margins or efficiency gains; two, it prevents a race to the bottom where competitors copy shrinkflation to avoid being undercut; three, it pushes brands to compete honestly on quality, size, or price instead of manipulating consumer perception.

Third, it protects trust in branded goods and preserves long-run demand. This matters because repeated deception creates consumer backlash, brand dilution, and regulatory distrust; once consumers believe a brand is gaming them, they switch to private label or discount alternatives, so enforcement can improve market functioning even if it slightly constrains short-term pricing flexibility.

opp_args.thesis: Aggressive shrinkflation regulation is overreach that raises compliance costs and reduces firms’ ability to respond to genuine input-cost shocks.
mechanisms: First, it increases the cost of passing through inflation. (1) Firms facing cocoa, energy, and logistics shocks need flexible ways to preserve viability; (2) forcing prominent wrapper redesigns or notices adds packaging, legal, and administrative costs; (3) those costs are ultimately passed on to consumers through higher shelf prices or reduced product availability.

Second, it can distort product innovation and portfolio management. (1) Companies may avoid smaller-format products even when consumers prefer lower absolute prices or portion sizes; (2) they may keep inefficient legacy sizes to avoid litigation risk; (3) this reduces experimentation and can lock consumers into worse-value offerings if firms cannot adjust pack sizes efficiently.

Third, the line between deception and ordinary price adjustment is blurry. (1) Many products have always had variable weights and formats across markets and time; (2) consumers can be informed through online channels, labels, and unit pricing rather than heavy-handed court intervention; (3) over-enforcement risks turning consumer law into a tool for punishing unpopular but economically rational responses to inflation.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether consumers can realistically detect hidden quantity cuts without legal intervention. Prop wins if you think packaging exploits bounded attention at scale; opp wins if you think the main problem is inflation itself and that regulation mostly adds cost rather than meaningfully changing consumer welfare.

cards.title: Trump’s Beijing Summit Risks Trading Taiwan Security for Chinese Help on Iran
cards.region: United States and China; Iran / Taiwan
cards.background: Donald Trump is due to arrive in Beijing on Wednesday evening for a two-day summit with Xi Jinping, his first visit to China as US president in nearly a decade. The visit comes as the US and China remain in a fragile tariff truce reached last autumn, while Washington is also trying to get Beijing to pressure Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and accept US peace terms after a war that has entered its third month. White House officials say Trump will travel with more than a dozen business leaders, including Elon Musk and Tim Cook, signaling continued economic engagement despite strategic rivalry.

prop_args.thesis: Trump should use the summit to cut a transactional deal with China that stabilizes the Iran crisis even if it requires tactical concessions on Taiwan and trade.
mechanisms: First, a deal with China is the fastest way to reduce the Iran war’s spillover costs. This is because (1) Beijing has leverage over Tehran through energy, shipping, and diplomatic channels; (2) the US is already struggling to turn a fragile ceasefire into a lasting settlement; and (3) reopening the Strait of Hormuz would immediately lower global energy prices and ease the 3.8% inflation pressure hitting American households.

Second, limited concessions on Taiwan or tariffs can be justified as bargaining chips rather than permanent retreats. Three reasons: one, the US-China relationship is already in a tariff truce, so a managed bargain can preserve stability; two, Trump can frame the summit as preventing a larger war and protecting American economic interests; three, business participation from Apple and Tesla shows both sides still want a working economic relationship, making a grand bargain politically and commercially feasible.

Third, prioritizing crisis management over symbolic deterrence is the better strategic choice in the short run. This matters because (1) the US cannot credibly fight Iran, deter China, and absorb inflationary shocks all at once; (2) a temporary de-escalation in East Asia buys time to rebuild US military and diplomatic credibility; and (3) avoiding a two-front confrontation reduces the risk of miscalculation that could spiral into a wider regional war.

opp_args.thesis: Trump should not trade away Taiwan credibility or strategic leverage because it would reward coercion and weaken US deterrence against China.
mechanisms: First, any concession on Taiwan creates a dangerous precedent of bargaining away allies for short-term crisis relief. One, China learns that military pressure and diplomatic leverage can extract US retrenchment; two, Taiwan and other US partners conclude American security guarantees are negotiable; three, that perception increases the odds of future coercion or even invasion because deterrence has been visibly weakened.

Second, a deal that depends on Chinese help against Iran is structurally unreliable. One, Beijing’s interests are not aligned with Washington’s and it may offer only symbolic pressure while preserving ties with Tehran; two, China can pocket concessions on tariffs or Taiwan without delivering meaningful compliance; three, the US then loses credibility in Asia while gaining little on the Middle East front.

Third, the summit risks domestic and alliance blowback that outweighs any temporary economic gain. One, abandoning hard lines on Taiwan would alarm Congress, the defense establishment, and regional allies like Japan; two, it would signal that US policy is driven by Trump’s need to repair prestige after the Iran war rather than by long-term strategy; three, once credibility is damaged, rebuilding it is far harder than maintaining a firm position in the first place.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the immediate payoff from de-escalating Iran outweighs the long-term cost of weakening deterrence in East Asia. The opposition has the structural advantage on credibility and precedent, but the proposition can win if it proves the Iran war is already imposing acute economic and security costs that make a transactional summit the least bad option.

THBT the US should prioritize de-escalation with China over defending every strategic red line in East Asia
THP a world where great powers are willing to bargain over regional security issues to end wider wars

cards.title: Settlement Corridor Demolitions Deepen West Bank Fragmentation and Displacement
cards.background: On 13 May 2026, Israel demolished 50 shops in al-Eizariya overnight, affecting the livelihoods of more than 200 families. The demolitions were carried out despite legal appeals to the Israeli Supreme Court. Israel has also earmarked land for a settlement-linked road corridor that would bisect the occupied West Bank and displace thousands of Bedouin villagers.

prop_args.thesis: Building settlement-linked infrastructure and demolishing Palestinian commercial sites entrenches occupation by physically fragmenting Palestinian territory and making a viable Palestinian state harder to sustain.
mechanisms: First, the road corridor creates territorial contiguity for settlements while destroying Palestinian contiguity. This is because (1) the road is designed to connect settlement blocs rather than local Palestinian communities, (2) it bisects the West Bank into disconnected enclaves, and (3) once movement is rerouted around settlement infrastructure, Palestinians face higher transport costs, longer travel times, and weaker internal trade networks.

Second, the demolitions produce economic displacement that compounds political displacement. Three reasons: one, 50 shops serving more than 200 families are not just buildings but local employment nodes; two, losing commercial space pushes households into debt, informal work, or migration; three, when livelihoods disappear, communities become less able to resist further land seizure and more vulnerable to coerced relocation.

Third, this normalizes unilateral facts on the ground that weaken future negotiations. This matters because (1) repeated infrastructure expansion signals that borders will be determined by force rather than talks, (2) it rewards settlement expansion with state-backed permanence, and (3) it makes any two-state settlement less credible by pre-emptively deciding key territorial questions.

opp_args.thesis: Israel can justify the road and demolitions as necessary security and administrative measures that improve mobility, enforce planning law, and reduce long-term conflict risk.
mechanisms: First, the state can argue the corridor serves security and control objectives. One, roads linked to settlements can allow faster military and emergency access across contested areas; two, centralized transport routes can reduce ad hoc movement through vulnerable zones; three, Israeli authorities can claim that territorial management is preferable to fragmented, unregulated development.

Second, the demolitions can be framed as lawful enforcement rather than arbitrary dispossession. One, the article notes legal appeals were made, implying the state is operating through formal institutions; two, governments routinely justify demolition of structures built without permits; three, if courts uphold the action, Israel can claim procedural legitimacy even if the outcome is politically controversial.

Third, supporters can argue infrastructure integration may improve the economy in the long run. One, better roads can lower logistics costs and connect labor markets; two, clearer transport corridors can reduce bottlenecks and uncertainty for commerce; three, if paired with broader arrangements, infrastructure can be presented as a prerequisite for stability rather than an obstacle to it.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the road is treated as neutral infrastructure or as a territorial instrument that locks in settlement expansion. Prop is stronger on structural irreversibility: once land is taken and communities are fragmented, the status quo becomes much harder to reverse, whereas Opp mostly relies on claims about security, legality, and future economic efficiency.

cards.title: Iran War Spending and Domestic Political Blowback Expose the Fiscal Limits of Prolonged Intervention
cards.background: The Pentagon now estimates the war with Iran has cost about $29 billion, up from $25 billion two weeks earlier. Officials told Congress that this figure does not include repairs to U.S. facilities hit by Iran; a CSIS adviser said those repairs could add at least another $4 billion. The Pentagon also plans to request supplemental funding, while GOP lawmakers are facing voter frustration over the conflict and its economic effects.

prop_args.thesis: The war with Iran is becoming a politically and fiscally unsustainable intervention that weakens U.S. domestic stability and strategic credibility.
mechanisms: First, the war imposes a direct fiscal shock that crowds out domestic priorities. This is because (1) the Pentagon already estimates $29 billion in costs, (2) repairs to damaged U.S. facilities could add at least another $4 billion, and (3) supplemental funding requests normalize open-ended war spending that competes with other budget items.

Second, the conflict creates political backlash that erodes coalition support for the administration. Three reasons: one, Republicans are already showing frustration over the lack of information from the White House; two, voters are seeing daily economic reminders of the war; three, an unpopular war heading into an election cycle makes legislators more risk-averse and less willing to sustain escalation.

Third, prolonged war increases the likelihood of strategic overreach. This matters because (1) the longer the conflict continues, the more sunk costs pressure leaders to stay engaged, (2) rising costs make exit politically harder, and (3) visible domestic strain signals weakness to adversaries who can outlast U.S. public tolerance.

opp_args.thesis: The war is costly, but the spending is manageable and necessary to protect U.S. security and deterrence.
mechanisms: First, the fiscal burden is large in absolute terms but still absorbable for the U.S. state. One, $29 billion is small relative to the overall federal budget and defense topline; two, supplemental appropriations are a standard wartime tool; three, repairing damaged facilities is a predictable cost of military operations rather than a reason to abandon them.

Second, the war may strengthen deterrence and reduce longer-term costs. One, showing willingness to pay now can prevent wider regional escalation later; two, failing to respond to Iranian attacks would invite future aggression against U.S. assets; three, a credible military posture can shorten conflicts by raising the adversary's expected costs.

Third, domestic political discomfort does not necessarily translate into policy failure. One, voters often tolerate security spending when framed as defense; two, congressional frustration is not the same as legislative refusal to fund the war; three, administrations can absorb short-term backlash if the strategic case remains persuasive.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the war's costs are a temporary security expense or the start of an open-ended fiscal and political drain. Prop wins if it proves the conflict is structurally unsustainable and erodes domestic support faster than it improves security; opp wins if it shows the spending is still manageable and buys deterrence that prevents a much larger war.

THBT the United States should prioritize ending the war in Iran over maintaining military pressure

cards.title: Brazil’s Amazon Land Demarcation Becomes a Test of Whether Indigenous Protection Can Survive Agribusiness Pressure
cards.background: Brazil has begun demarcating the Pardo River Kawahiva Indigenous territory, a 410,000-hectare area between Mato Grosso and Amazonas, after the existence of the uncontacted Kawahiva was confirmed in 1999. The process has taken 27 years and still requires the president’s signature for full recognition, while agribusiness-linked groups continue to challenge it in court. The territory is home to about 290 Kawahiva people and is one of several areas in the Amazon facing pressure from farming expansion, land grabs, illegal logging and mining. Brazil’s presidential election is due in October, with polls showing a close race between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro.

prop_args.thesis: Formal demarcation is the only credible way to protect uncontacted peoples because it turns vague recognition into enforceable territorial sovereignty.
mechanisms: First, demarcation creates a legally legible boundary that the state can actually police. This is because (1) unmarked land is easy to reclassify as vacant or underutilized, (2) geodetic markers and mapped borders give Funai and federal police a basis for enforcement, and (3) courts and regulators can then treat incursions as clear violations rather than ambiguous disputes.

Second, it reduces the economic incentives for invasion by making extraction riskier and more expensive. Three reasons: one, agribusiness and land-grabbers rely on uncertainty to expand the agricultural frontier; two, formal recognition strengthens injunctions against logging, mining and settlement; three, buffer zones make edge encroachment harder and slow the spread of deforestation.

Third, it is the only policy that preserves the physical and cultural survival of uncontacted groups. This matters because contact with armed outsiders brings disease, violence and displacement, and the article shows the Kawahiva have already faced massacres, deaths linked to land disputes, and sustained pressure from rural violence.

prop_args.thesis: Protecting Indigenous territories is a high-value climate and governance intervention because it prevents deforestation more effectively than many state-led conservation schemes.
mechanisms: First, Indigenous lands function as low-deforestation enforcement zones. This is because (1) local presence deters illegal logging and mining, (2) community-backed territorial claims make occupation harder to normalize, and (3) the article notes Indigenous lands have recorded the lowest rates of deforestation in the Amazon in recent years.

Second, demarcation improves state capacity by concentrating scarce enforcement resources on clearly defined areas. Three reasons: one, Funai and police can prioritize a mapped territory rather than scattered claims; two, permanent markers reduce monitoring costs; three, legal certainty makes it easier to coordinate buffer zones and rapid response to incursions.

Third, the broader payoff is that protecting one territory creates a precedent for the rest of the Amazon. This matters because the article identifies other pending areas like Piripkura, Ituna-Itatá and Jacareúba-Katawixi, so successful demarcation can unlock a wider protection cascade.

opp_args.thesis: Demarcation on paper is insufficient and may even intensify conflict if the state cannot credibly enforce the borders it creates.
mechanisms: First, formal recognition can provoke backlash from powerful land interests. One, agribusiness-linked groups have already launched repeated legal challenges; two, clearer boundaries can harden opposition by turning a political dispute into a direct property conflict; three, if enforcement is weak, the symbolic victory may invite more aggressive incursions to test state resolve.

Second, the policy can fail operationally because the state lacks the manpower and logistics to protect remote territories. One, Funai staff and federal police must secure vast forest areas plus geodetic markers; two, the article explicitly says safety is difficult during and after demarcation; three, without sustained funding, borders become lines on a map that armed actors ignore.

Third, prioritizing demarcation may not solve the broader drivers of Amazon destruction. One, land pressure comes from the agricultural frontier, mining and illegal logging across the region; two, if national land-use incentives remain unchanged, actors simply shift to other vulnerable areas; three, the policy can become a narrow conservation fix that leaves the underlying political economy intact.

opp_args.thesis: A strategy focused on formal demarcation can be too slow and legalistic to protect uncontacted peoples in time.
mechanisms: First, the process itself is vulnerable to delay and reversal. One, this case took 27 years from confirmation to demarcation; two, full recognition still depends on presidential approval; three, an election could bring a government less committed to Indigenous protection.

Second, legal recognition does not automatically protect groups that remain unconfirmed or unmapped. One, the government says there are 115 isolated groups but only 29 confirmed; two, many communities may be invisible to the state until it is too late; three, a framework centered on formal demarcation can miss the most vulnerable populations.

Third, the opportunity cost is high because every year of delay increases the chance of irreversible harm. One, uncontacted peoples face disease and violence from outsiders; two, the article references existing massacres and deaths tied to land disputes; three, a slow legal process can be functionally equivalent to abandonment.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between legal certainty and enforcement capacity: prop wins if the question is whether demarcation is the necessary precondition for any durable protection, while opp wins if the round is about whether the state can actually defend remote land against organized economic interests. This argument wins because the article shows both the value of clear borders and the fragility of implementation, so the side that best controls the enforcement story has the structural advantage.

THP a world where Indigenous land protection is treated as a non-negotiable state policy insulated from electoral change
THBT developing countries should empower Indigenous land agencies over agribusiness interests in frontier regions

cards.title: Trump-Style Currency Politics Raises Fears of Politicized U.S. Money and Institutional Erosion
cards.background: The article is about speculation triggered by a social media post suggesting Donald Trump could appear on U.S. banknotes. The only concrete factual context provided is a Bloomberg photo caption from April 24, 2025 showing Trump with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent during a White House lunch with Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store. The issue sits at the intersection of monetary symbolism, executive power, and the perceived independence of U.S. financial institutions.

prop_args.thesis: Putting a sitting or former president on U.S. banknotes politicizes the currency and weakens confidence in the neutrality of core economic institutions.
mechanisms: First, it turns money into a partisan symbol rather than a national one. This is because (1) banknotes are used by every citizen and foreign holder, (2) the design of currency is supposed to signal continuity across administrations, and (3) once one leader is canonized on money, future leaders face pressure to do the same, normalizing personalization of the state.

Second, it erodes institutional trust by blurring the line between the presidency and the Treasury. Three reasons: one, it suggests the executive can repurpose state symbols for self-branding; two, it creates the perception that monetary institutions are responsive to political loyalty rather than technocratic standards; three, it invites markets to read symbolic actions as a precursor to more substantive interference in fiscal or monetary governance.

Third, it creates a precedent for broader democratic backsliding through personality cult politics. This matters because the symbolic capture of state assets is often an early-stage mechanism of institutional degradation: once the leader is normalized as the face of the state, opposition is framed as anti-national, and checks on executive overreach become easier to delegitimize.

opp_args.thesis: Changing or discussing currency imagery is mostly symbolic and can be used to strengthen national identity without materially harming economic institutions.
mechanisms: First, the practical economic effects are minimal because banknote imagery does not determine inflation, interest rates, or Treasury financing. One, markets care far more about fiscal credibility and Fed policy than portrait selection; two, many countries regularly update notes without institutional crisis; three, public debate over symbols can be absorbed as ordinary political theater.

Second, it can be framed as democratic expression rather than personalization of power. One, elected governments have authority over national symbols; two, if the public supports the change, it reflects popular sovereignty rather than elite capture; three, the symbolism may be temporary and reversible after leadership changes.

Third, it may even reinforce legitimacy if it is seen as honoring a major political figure. One, national currencies often commemorate founders or transformative leaders; two, such imagery can increase public attachment to the currency; three, in a polarized environment, a unifying patriotic narrative may matter more than abstract concerns about symbolism.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between symbolic institutional erosion and material economic harm. Prop wins if it shows that currency design is a high-salience state symbol and that politicizing it normalizes executive personalization; opp wins if it keeps the clash in the realm of harmless optics and argues markets and institutions are driven by harder fundamentals.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would place Donald Trump on US banknotes
THBT governments should not place living or former political leaders on national currency
THP a world where national currency design is insulated from executive influence

cards.title: Closing Refuge for Afghan Allies Turns Asylum Into a Bribery-Driven Escape Lottery
cards.background: Safia Noori and Fakhruddin Elham are former Afghan special forces members who fought alongside U.S. troops and fled Taliban persecution after Kabul fell in 2021. After living as refugees in Pakistan, they were caught between Pakistan’s mass deportation campaign against Afghans and the Trump administration’s decision to close the door on Afghan resettlement. Spain eventually approved them for “international protection” on March 25, but they still had to navigate Pakistani exit permits, fines, bribes, and airport harassment before boarding a Turkish Airlines flight to Madrid on April 10.

prop_args.thesis: When major states shut legal pathways for refugees, they do not reduce movement; they force it into black markets, corruption, and life-threatening improvisation.
mechanisms: First, closing formal resettlement channels pushes desperate refugees into informal brokers and bribery networks. This is because (1) the official route becomes inaccessible, (2) people still facing persecution cannot simply stay put, and (3) intermediaries can extract monopoly rents by controlling scarce documents like visas and exit permits.

Second, restrictive host-state policies convert refugees into easy targets for police abuse and deportation. Three reasons: one, undocumented status makes every checkpoint a risk of arrest; two, bureaucrats can demand extra payments because the victim has no legal recourse; three, fear of deportation weakens bargaining power and makes compliance the default.

Third, the humanitarian cost is not abstract but immediate and lethal. This matters because the family in the article was repeatedly one delay away from being sent back to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, showing that asylum policy is literally a survival mechanism rather than a symbolic gesture.

prop_args.thesis: States that abandon allied refugees destroy the credibility of future security partnerships and make local cooperation with Western forces far harder.
mechanisms: First, allies update their expectations about whether promises of protection are real. This is because (1) Afghan commandos and interpreters see that service to the West does not guarantee rescue, (2) future partners in conflict zones anticipate abandonment, and (3) that reduces willingness to cooperate with U.S. or European missions in the next war.

Second, betrayal creates a reputational spillover beyond Afghanistan. Three reasons: one, armed groups use these cases as propaganda to portray Western commitments as disposable; two, local elites hedge by avoiding visible alignment with the West; three, the West loses soft power precisely where it needs trust most.

Third, the policy damages long-run strategic capacity. This matters because counterinsurgency, intelligence gathering, and evacuation operations all depend on credible promises to local allies, and once credibility is lost it is expensive to rebuild.

opp_args.thesis: States are entitled to tighten refugee and migration controls when they face domestic capacity limits, security concerns, and political backlash.
mechanisms: First, governments have to preserve border control and administrative capacity. One, large inflows can overwhelm asylum systems and housing; two, weak screening can create security risks if hostile actors exploit refugee routes; three, governments need to prioritize citizens and legally admitted residents when resources are finite.

Second, restrictive policy can be defended as a response to domestic political legitimacy. One, voters often punish governments that appear unable to control migration; two, if asylum policy becomes too permissive it can fuel populist backlash and destabilize democratic coalitions; three, elected governments may need to signal enforcement to keep broader support for immigration overall.

Third, host states like Pakistan may argue they are not responsible for indefinitely absorbing another country’s collapse. One, they already host millions of Afghans; two, prolonged refugee presence creates local labor, housing, and policing pressures; three, without burden-sharing from richer states, unilateral openness can be politically and fiscally unsustainable.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between immediate human survival and state claims to control borders. Prop wins if the round prioritizes irreversible harm and the fact that legal closure predictably creates corruption and death-risk; opp wins if the bench is persuaded that states cannot be expected to absorb open-ended refugee obligations without domestic collapse or security blowback.

THBT host states should be required to provide safe passage for refugees awaiting third-country asylum
THP a world in which wealthy states are legally bound to resettle local allies from failed interventions
THBT Pakistan should be sanctioned for mass deportations of Afghan refugees

cards.title: Streeting Challenge Exposes Labour’s Fragile Succession and Risks Government Paralysis
cards.background: On 13 May 2026, the Guardian reported that allies of Health Secretary Wes Streeting said he was preparing to resign and mount a leadership challenge against Prime Minister Keir Starmer as early as Thursday. Under Labour rules, a challenger needs the support of 81 MPs to formally trigger a contest; Downing Street said Streeting did not yet have the numbers, while Streeting allies claimed he believed he could secure them. The report followed Starmer’s “put up or shut up” ultimatum to cabinet ministers and renewed calls from Streeting ally Zubir Ahmed, who had resigned as a minister the previous day, for Starmer to step down.

prop_args.thesis: A successful Streeting challenge could restore Labour’s governing authority by replacing a weakened leader before internal collapse spreads into policy paralysis.
mechanisms: First, a leadership change can reset party discipline and stop the bleeding of elite defections. This is because (1) MPs who are currently hedging get a clear centre of gravity, (2) cabinet resignations stop being read as a signal of terminal decline, and (3) the party can reassemble around a single authority rather than multiple rival factions.

Second, Streeting can improve Labour’s electoral and parliamentary credibility by offering a more viable public face. Three reasons: one, he is already a senior cabinet figure with national profile, two, a new leader can claim a fresh mandate rather than inheriting Starmer’s damaged authority, and three, opponents inside and outside the party have less time to frame the government as exhausted and directionless.

Third, the contest itself can be used to force a strategic correction in policy and messaging. This matters because a leadership challenge exposes what MPs actually want from the government, allowing the winner to pivot on unpopular decisions, rebuild trust with backbenchers, and reduce the risk that a demoralised administration drifts into permanent crisis management.

opp_args.thesis: A Streeting challenge would deepen Labour’s instability, making the government look self-absorbed and weakening its ability to govern.
mechanisms: First, a leadership contest consumes time, attention, and political capital at the exact moment the government needs to project competence. 1) Ministers stop focusing on policy delivery and start counting votes, 2) media coverage becomes dominated by factionalism rather than governing, and 3) every decision is interpreted through the lens of who is backing whom.

Second, the challenge can permanently fracture Labour’s coalition even if Streeting loses. 1) Starmer loyalists will distrust challengers and their allies, 2) Streeting supporters may feel alienated and obstructive after defeat, and 3) the party may emerge with no clear consensus on direction, making future rebellions more likely.

Third, replacing Starmer does not guarantee improved governance because the underlying problems may be structural rather than personal. 1) Labour may still face weak public support, 2) a new leader may inherit the same policy constraints and parliamentary arithmetic, and 3) a rushed coup can elevate short-term factional advantage over long-term competence.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether a leadership challenge restores authority faster than it destroys it. Pro-change arguments win if Starmer is already so weakened that only a reset can prevent ongoing collapse; anti-change arguments win if the contest itself becomes the main source of paralysis and factional damage.
motion_areas: TH, as a governing party, would replace a failing leader even mid-term
THBT political parties should allow easier leadership challenges during government crises
THP a world where cabinet ministers can trigger leadership contests with lower thresholds

cards.title: Starmer’s public-service overhaul trades institutional reform for growth, control, and tighter migration enforcement
cards.background: On 13 May 2026, Keir Starmer used the King’s Speech to set out a major legislative programme for the next parliamentary session. The package includes bills to abolish NHS England, overhaul special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) provision, limit jury trials, introduce digital ID for immigration checks, end the leasehold system in England and Wales, and make it harder for migrants to gain settled status. Ministers also plan a bill to encourage regulators to consider growth and to lay the groundwork for closer alignment with European regulations.

prop_args.thesis: Starmer’s package is a necessary state-capacity reset that can improve service delivery, reduce legal and administrative bottlenecks, and create a more investable, higher-growth UK economy.
mechanisms: First, abolishing NHS England and tightening ministerial control can reduce duplication and blame-shifting. This is because (1) the current split between the Department of Health and NHS England creates overlapping command structures, (2) clearer accountability lets ministers force faster prioritisation of waiting lists and workforce decisions, and (3) centralised control makes it easier to reallocate resources toward the highest-pressure services rather than preserving bureaucracy for its own sake.

Second, reforming SEND provision and limiting automatic entitlement growth can stop a fiscally unsustainable spending spiral. Three reasons: one, EHCP expansion has pushed local-authority budgets into crisis, two, schools are better placed than tribunals and paperwork to identify many needs early and cheaply, and three, shifting responsibility to mainstream schools can encourage earlier intervention instead of costly late-stage escalation.

Third, the growth-and-regulation agenda can unlock investment by reducing legal uncertainty and planning friction. This matters because (1) regulators being told to weigh growth changes the default from pure risk aversion to balancing costs and benefits, (2) closer alignment with EU rules lowers compliance costs for exporters and reduces post-Brexit fragmentation, and (3) a more predictable regulatory environment improves business confidence, which is especially important when the UK is trying to raise productivity and living standards.

opp_args.thesis: The package centralises power while weakening rights and public-service guarantees, so it risks making services harsher, less accountable, and politically more polarised without solving underlying capacity problems.
mechanisms: First, cutting access to EHCPs and shifting decisions to schools can ration support rather than fix it. One, schools already face staff and funding shortages, so they may under-identify needs to protect budgets; two, families lose legally enforceable entitlements and are pushed into informal appeals; three, children with complex needs may be mainstreamed without adequate support, worsening attainment and mental-health outcomes.

Second, restricting jury trials and tightening settlement rules can erode legitimacy and deepen distrust in the state. One, jury limits weaken a core safeguard against overreach in serious criminal cases; two, immigration restrictions framed around control can alienate Labour MPs and minority communities, making implementation politically unstable; three, if people perceive reforms as punitive rather than fair, compliance and social cohesion fall.

Third, the reforms may not deliver the promised efficiency gains because structural shortages, not institutional design alone, are the binding constraint. This is because (1) NHS waiting lists are driven by staffing, capital, and demand pressures that abolishing NHS England does not solve, (2) courts backlogs require judges, courtrooms, and legal aid rather than just procedural tweaks, and (3) housing and leasehold reform are slow-burn changes that will not quickly offset the political cost of attacking entrenched rights.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether institutional centralisation actually translates into better outcomes, or whether it just concentrates blame while stripping away safeguards. Prop wins if the judge prioritises state capacity and fiscal sustainability; Opp wins if they show the reforms mainly ration scarcity and trade away rights for uncertain efficiency gains.

cards.title: Trump-China Summit Turns Iran War Into a Bargaining Chip in Great-Power Trade Diplomacy
cards.background: President Trump arrived in China on Wednesday for a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. According to NPR, the war in Iran, trade policies, and Taiwan were expected to be the major topics of discussion. The article frames the summit as a high-stakes meeting where Washington and Beijing may link regional security issues to broader economic and strategic bargaining.

prop_args.thesis: A Trump-Xi summit that links Iran to trade gives the US leverage to force China into constraining Tehran and stabilizing a wider regional war.
mechanisms: First, the US can trade economic concessions for Chinese cooperation on Iran. This is because (1) China is highly exposed to US market access and tariff policy, (2) Beijing has incentives to avoid a Middle East escalation that disrupts energy flows, and (3) a direct leader-level summit creates a rare moment for side payments and quid pro quo diplomacy.

Second, bringing Iran into the same bargaining space as trade increases pressure on China to act as a responsible stakeholder. Three reasons: one, China cannot easily separate its commercial interests from its strategic interests when the US is simultaneously negotiating tariffs and Taiwan; two, Beijing gains reputational costs if it is seen as shielding a war sponsor while seeking economic normalization; three, coordinated pressure can raise the cost of continued Iranian escalation through diplomacy, sanctions enforcement, or reduced material support.

Third, even partial Chinese restraint on Iran can meaningfully reduce war intensity. This matters because China is one of the few actors with enough economic and diplomatic ties to influence Iranian calculations, so any shift in Beijing's posture can constrain financing, oil purchases, and political backing that sustain the conflict.

opp_args.thesis: Mixing Iran, trade, and Taiwan in one summit weakens US strategy by turning a security crisis into a transactional bargaining game that China can exploit.
mechanisms: First, issue-linkage gives China leverage to demand concessions without changing its Iran policy. one, Beijing can offer symbolic cooperation while extracting trade relief; two, the US risks paying twice by conceding on tariffs and still getting little on Iran; three, China can frame any limited help as a diplomatic favor rather than a binding commitment.

Second, the summit incentivizes China to harden its position on Iran and Taiwan as counter-pressure. one, if Washington uses Iran to pressure Beijing, China has reason to respond by signaling support for Tehran or by becoming less cooperative on regional security; two, tying Taiwan into the same conversation makes the talks more zero-sum and reduces trust; three, the result is strategic entanglement that makes de-escalation harder, not easier.

Third, leader-level bargaining can normalize great-power spheres of influence over smaller states. one, Iran becomes a pawn in US-China competition rather than an independent actor whose war should be resolved on its own terms; two, this encourages transactional diplomacy over principled nonproliferation or humanitarian restraint; three, it can entrench a world where major powers trade away regional stability for bilateral gains.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether issue-linkage creates leverage or creates vulnerability. Pro wins if the summit produces even modest Chinese restraint on Iran, but Opp has the structural advantage that China can pocket trade concessions while offering only symbolic cooperation, making the bargaining asymmetrical.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would link trade concessions to cooperation on Iran in summit diplomacy
THBT great powers should use economic negotiations to secure security outcomes from rivals
THP a world where US-China summits bundle trade, Taiwan, and Middle East security into one bargaining package

cards.title: China–U.S. Economic Competition Hardens Into a Structural Rivalry Over Trade, Technology, and Industrial Power
cards.background: This NPR piece is a short interview with Chinese economist Dan Wang on the competing economic interests of China and the United States. The article frames the relationship as one of direct economic rivalry rather than simple interdependence, with both states pursuing advantage in trade, technology, industrial policy, and supply chains. The text provided does not include detailed policy announcements or new quantitative data, but it clearly centers the strategic conflict between the two economies.

prop_args.thesis: The U.S. and China are locked in a zero-sum economic rivalry, so decoupling and industrial policy are rational responses to prevent strategic dependence.
mechanisms: First, supply-chain dependence becomes a national security vulnerability. This is because (1) critical inputs like semiconductors, batteries, and rare earth processing can be restricted in a crisis, (2) firms optimize for cost rather than resilience, so market integration concentrates risk in a few chokepoints, and (3) once one side can weaponize access, the other side has to pay the cost of redundancy to avoid coercion.

Second, competition over technology creates a race for strategic dominance. Three reasons: one, whoever controls frontier technologies sets standards and captures downstream industries; two, state support for AI, chips, and advanced manufacturing compounds over time through learning curves and scale; three, allowing unrestricted transfer risks accelerating a rival’s military and industrial capacity.

Third, economic separation can preserve bargaining power and domestic legitimacy. This matters because a government that can show it is protecting jobs, firms, and critical infrastructure is less vulnerable to domestic backlash, and because a clearer rivalry framework reduces the illusion that commercial engagement alone will moderate geopolitical conflict.

opp_args.thesis: Despite rivalry, deep economic interdependence still lowers the risk of conflict and makes cooperation more valuable than decoupling.
mechanisms: First, trade and investment create mutual costs that discipline escalation. One, both economies rely on each other for markets, capital, and intermediate goods; two, disruption raises prices and hurts consumers and exporters on both sides; three, those domestic losses create lobbying pressure against sanctions spirals and military escalation.

Second, decoupling is inefficient and can backfire strategically. One, forcing firms to duplicate supply chains raises costs and slows innovation; two, protectionism can entrench domestic monopolies and reduce competitiveness; three, if allies and firms see U.S.-China policy as arbitrary, they hedge rather than align, weakening the very coalition needed to balance China.

Third, engagement preserves channels for crisis management and global public goods. One, climate, financial stability, and pandemic response require coordination between the two largest economies; two, economic ties create communication networks that reduce miscalculation; three, even rivals need rules and institutions to prevent tit-for-tat retaliation from spilling into broader instability.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether economic interdependence is a stabilizer or a vulnerability. Prop wins if you believe strategic sectors are so coercible that resilience and decoupling matter more than efficiency; Opp wins if you think the costs of fragmentation and the value of crisis communication outweigh the benefits of insulation.
motion_areas: TH, as the United States, would pursue economic decoupling from China
THBT major powers should prioritize supply-chain resilience over free trade
THP a world where the U.S. and China maintain deep economic interdependence despite strategic rivalry

cards.title: AI Datacentre Boom Forces UK and US Into Grid Strain, Higher Bills, and Fossil-Fuel Backsliding
cards.background: Datacentres now consume 5.9% of electricity in the UK and 6% in the US, according to research cited by the International Data Center Association (IDCA). The IDCA says global investment in datacentres is approaching $1tn annually, with electricity use rising 15% worldwide in the past two years; in the UK, the grid-connection queue grew by 460% in the first half of 2025. The UK government estimated in early 2025 that datacentres used 2.5% of electricity and predicted a fourfold increase by 2030, while the IEA says energy use rose 17% in 2025 against 3% growth in global electricity demand.

prop_args.thesis: Governments should actively constrain and regulate datacentre expansion because the AI boom is now a macroeconomic and infrastructure externality, not just a private-sector growth story.
mechanisms: First, unrestricted datacentre growth crowds out scarce grid capacity. This is because (1) the UK already has energy shortages and a 460% rise in the grid-connection queue in H1 2025, (2) datacentres are already taking 5.9% of UK electricity and 6% in the US, and (3) every additional large facility locks in long lead times for households and productive industry that need the same transmission capacity.

Second, the boom raises consumer and fiscal costs through infrastructure bottlenecks. Three reasons: one, grid upgrades and new generation are capital-intensive and are ultimately socialized through bills or public spending; two, developers are already waiting years for national grid connections, which signals a supply crunch and higher marginal costs; three, the sector's $1tn annual investment scale means even small inefficiencies or overbuilds have economy-wide price effects.

Third, regulation is justified because the sector has major negative spillovers and weak self-correction. This matters because (1) 13% of US datacentre consumption is 'zombie' usage, wasting more than 3GW, (2) firms have incentives to understate emissions and overstate benefits, as shown by reporting on Google-linked projects in the UK, and (3) without transparency and environmental impact assessments, communities bear the water, pollution, and land-use costs while firms capture the upside.

opp_args.thesis: Datacentres should be expanded, not constrained, because they are critical infrastructure that raises productivity and the real problem is energy supply, not digital demand.
mechanisms: First, datacentres are a necessary input into modern economic activity. One, they power cloud services, AI, payments, logistics, and communications that raise productivity across the whole economy; two, the reported $1tn annual investment reflects genuine demand for high-value digital infrastructure; three, restricting supply would slow innovation and push compute capacity to less regulated jurisdictions.

Second, the right policy response is to build more energy, not cap datacentre growth. This is because (1) the bottleneck is grid and generation capacity, not the existence of datacentres themselves, (2) the sector can be paired with new renewable, nuclear, or flexible demand investments, and (3) better planning and connection reform can absorb demand without sacrificing growth.

Third, the environmental critique is overstated relative to the efficiency gains from digitalization. Three reasons: one, the global average datacentre share is still 2%, so the UK and US are high but not uniquely unsustainable; two, centralizing compute in datacentres can be more efficient than fragmented on-premise servers; three, AI and cloud tools can reduce waste in other sectors, offsetting part of the electricity footprint.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether datacentres are treated as productive infrastructure or as a classic congestion externality. Prop has the stronger structural case if the round is about public policy because the grid is finite in the short run and the costs are immediate and localized, while opp relies on future efficiency and growth gains that are harder to guarantee.

THBT governments should require AI datacentres to bear the full cost of their energy and water externalities
THP a world in which datacentre expansion is subject to strict environmental impact assessments and transparency rules
THBT the state should prioritize household and industrial electricity access over datacentre growth

cards.title: Russia’s New ICBM Test Deepens the Post-Treaty Nuclear Arms Race With the West
cards.background: Russia test-fired a new intercontinental ballistic missile on Tuesday as part of its nuclear modernization program, and President Vladimir Putin said the Sarmat missile would enter combat service by the end of the year. The missile is intended to replace about 40 Soviet-built Voyevoda missiles; Putin claimed it has a range of more than 35,000 kilometers and can penetrate missile defenses. The launch comes after the last remaining Russia-U.S. nuclear arms pact expired in February, leaving no caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than 50 years.

prop_args.thesis: Russia’s missile test makes the world less safe by accelerating a destabilizing nuclear arms race and weakening the remaining incentives for restraint.
mechanisms: First, it pushes the system into a classic security dilemma. This is because (1) Russia frames the missile as a response to U.S. missile defense, (2) the U.S. and allies read the launch as coercive escalation and respond with more modernization, and (3) each side’s defensive move is interpreted as offensive preparation, which creates a self-reinforcing cycle of buildup.

Second, it erodes the already thin arms-control architecture. Three reasons: one, the last Russia-U.S. nuclear pact expired in February, so there are now no formal caps on deployed arsenals; two, publicized tests like Sarmat normalize unconstrained competition and make future limits politically harder to sell domestically; three, the more systems are fielded, the more bargaining leverage each side loses, reducing the chance of a new treaty.

Third, it increases crisis instability and miscalculation risk. This matters because a missile advertised as able to evade defenses and carry multiple warheads shortens decision time in a crisis, encourages launch-on-warning postures, and makes leaders more likely to assume they must use weapons early before their arsenal is degraded.

prop_args.thesis: Russia’s modernization strengthens coercive nuclear signaling, which increases pressure on Ukraine and deters Western support.
mechanisms: First, it gives Putin a credible intimidation tool in the Ukraine war. This is because (1) he has repeatedly brandished nuclear threats since 2022, (2) the test is timed alongside claims that the war is nearing an end, and (3) the message to Western capitals is that continued support risks escalation beyond the conventional battlefield.

Second, it widens the gap between Russian rhetoric and Western willingness to escalate. Three reasons: one, the new missile is presented as capable of penetrating any missile defense, which makes reassurance harder; two, European states facing Oreshnik’s 5,000-kilometer range have stronger incentives to self-deter; three, allies may become more cautious about supplying advanced systems to Ukraine if they fear triggering a broader confrontation.

Third, it helps Russia preserve strategic parity despite sanctions and battlefield costs. This matters because nuclear modernization allows Moscow to compensate for conventional weakness, keep elite confidence in the regime, and signal that Russia remains a great power even if the war in Ukraine is costly.

opp_args.thesis: The test is mostly symbolic: it does not materially change the balance of power, and Russia is using nuclear theater to compensate for weakness.
mechanisms: First, the missile may not be operationally decisive. One, the article says Sarmat had only one known successful test before this and reportedly suffered a massive explosion in an abortive 2024 test; two, a weapons system that is still being tested does not immediately alter battlefield realities; three, Russia already has a large nuclear arsenal, so adding one more platform is marginal rather than transformative.

Second, the launch is primarily propaganda and deterrence messaging. One, Putin has repeatedly used nuclear rhetoric since 2022 to shape Western behavior; two, the timing alongside claims that the Ukraine war is ending suggests domestic political theater; three, exaggerated claims about being 'the most powerful missile in the world' are meant to project strength, not necessarily reflect usable military advantage.

Third, Western responses are likely to be limited and already priced in. This matters because (1) the U.S. has long been modernizing its arsenal in response to Russia, (2) allies already assume Russia will continue nuclear signaling, and (3) absent a direct treaty violation or deployment change, the test may produce headlines without changing actual policy.

opp_args.thesis: Nuclear modernization can stabilize deterrence by preserving parity and reducing incentives for a first strike.
mechanisms: First, maintaining a survivable second-strike capability can make deterrence more credible. One, Russia says the Sarmat replaces aging Soviet-era Voyevoda missiles; two, modernizing outdated systems can reduce the risk that an adversary believes it can disarm Russia cheaply; three, credible retaliation can deter both nuclear coercion and conventional escalation.

Second, the launch can be read as a response to U.S. missile defense rather than an offensive step. One, Russia explicitly argues it is adapting to the U.S. missile shield after Washington withdrew from the 2001 pact; two, if both sides believe the other can intercept retaliation, they have stronger incentives to maintain stable parity; three, modernization can therefore preserve the logic of mutual vulnerability that underpins deterrence.

Third, clearer and more capable arsenals can reduce ambiguity in crisis. This matters because (1) if each side knows the other retains a robust retaliatory capability, (2) the temptation to gamble on a first strike falls, and (3) stable deterrence can prevent conventional wars from spilling into nuclear exchange.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether modernization is read as stabilizing deterrence or as accelerating an unconstrained arms race. Prop has the stronger structural claim because the treaty collapse, explicit missile-defense counterframing, and repeated signaling around Ukraine all create a live escalation spiral rather than a one-off technical upgrade.

cards.title: Iran War Exposes How Geopolitical Shocks Can Rewire Consumer Supply Chains in Japan
cards.background: Tokyo-based Calbee Inc. said it will switch 14 snack products to black-and-white packaging starting May 25 because the war in Iran has disrupted supplies of an ingredient used in colored ink. The company, founded in 1949 and employing more than 5,000 people, said the move is meant to maintain a stable supply of products while it adapts to changing geopolitical conditions. Japan relies almost entirely on imported oil and is already facing pressure on naphtha, an oil-derived input used in plastics and ink, as the Middle East war and closure of the Strait of Hormuz raise costs and shortages.

prop_args.thesis: Geopolitical conflict now imposes real economic costs on advanced consumer economies by disrupting even mundane inputs, forcing firms to trade off branding, margins, and supply stability.
mechanisms: First, the war creates upstream input scarcity. This is because (1) the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and wider Middle East disruption tighten oil-linked supply chains, (2) Japan depends almost entirely on imported oil, and (3) naphtha-derived materials used in ink and plastics become harder and more expensive to source.

Second, firms respond by degrading non-essential product features to preserve core output. Three reasons: one, packaging color is cheaper to cut than production volume; two, simplifying packaging reduces dependence on constrained inputs; three, this lets Calbee keep shelves stocked rather than risk shortages or price spikes.

Third, this shows why supply-chain resilience is a macroeconomic issue, not just a corporate one. This matters because (1) repeated shocks force firms to redesign products and logistics, (2) consumers face hidden inflation through lower-quality goods and higher costs, and (3) economies become more vulnerable to external conflict even when they are not direct belligerents.

opp_args.thesis: This is a manageable supply-chain adjustment, not a systemic economic crisis, because firms and governments can absorb the shock through stockpiles, substitution, and product redesign.
mechanisms: First, the immediate impact is limited because the affected input is packaging ink, not the snack itself. One, Calbee says the contents remain unchanged; two, only 14 products are switching packaging; three, the company can preserve sales while waiting for supply conditions to normalize.

Second, Japan has buffers that reduce the risk of broader economic damage. One, the government says it has oil reserves and has worked to calm markets; two, large firms can reroute procurement or substitute materials; three, the change may be temporary, so the shock does not necessarily translate into lasting inflation or output losses.

Third, firms can turn scarcity into adaptation rather than decline. One, monochrome packaging can lower complexity and costs; two, consumers may care more about product quality than packaging color; three, the episode may accelerate more resilient sourcing strategies without meaningfully harming aggregate welfare.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether you treat this as a symbolic packaging change or evidence of deeper import dependence. Prop wins if it proves that even low-value consumer goods are now hostage to geopolitical shocks, because that implies broad economy-wide fragility; opp wins if it narrows the impact to a temporary, substitutable input problem with limited welfare loss.
